title: Bailout

jokes.text: These kids are renting my old clothes like they're going out of style. Which they never will.
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching Rent-A-Swag as a successful business venture
jokes.punchline: "Which they never will" — his total lack of irony about his own fashion ego
jokes.explanation: The self-correction that isn't a correction at all — Tom genuinely believes his fashion is timeless. The beat is quick and perfectly in character. Solid opener that establishes Tom's delusional self-confidence economically.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Which they never will. My fashion sense is timeless. I'm a trendsetter. People see what I'm wearing and they think, 'I need to dress like that guy.'

jokes.text: Oh, 'day-yay-yam,' it is kind of a sausage party in here. For the record, would hit it, would hit, would hit. Hard pass.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is introduced as a new sales associate at a clothing store
jokes.punchline: She immediately rates every male customer sexually, then hard-passes on one — her moral scale is entirely about attractiveness
jokes.explanation: Our first introduction to Mona-Lisa as a character; the joke is that she's so unapologetically inappropriate that she treats a store full of teen customers as a dating pool. The 'hard pass' punctuation makes it land. Funny but relies somewhat on shock value.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at all these guys. Let me just... *checks out each customer* Okay, that one's a solid 7, this one's a 4, oh that guy's definitely a 9...

jokes.text: My twin sister, from the same mister.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio reveals Mona-Lisa is his sister
jokes.punchline: "From the same mister" — a rhyming, oddly specific way of saying they share a father, with Jean-Ralphio's signature musical delivery
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable, deeply in character — Jean-Ralphio communicates everything in musical rhymes and this lands perfectly. 'From the same mister' is an original construction that only he would say. Strong character integration elevates what could be a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: We're the same mister!

jokes.text: Thank you so much for hiring Mona-Lisa. It means so much to me. Even though, honestly, she's... ♪ The wo-o-orst. She is the worst person in the world. Huge skank. Terrible.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio sincerely thanks Tom for hiring his sister
jokes.punchline: He seamlessly pivots to singing and enthusiastically cataloguing her flaws, then thanks Tom again — the warmth and the condemnation coexist without contradiction
jokes.explanation: One of the best Jean-Ralphio moments in the series. The structure is perfect: genuine gratitude → sung insult → more insults → back to gratitude. Only Jean-Ralphio would simultaneously love and publicly trash his sister in a single breath. 'Huge skank. Terrible.' delivered deadpan after singing is inspired. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, Tom, I just want to say thank you so much for hiring my sister Mona-Lisa. That's real generous of you, man. I appreciate it.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: But real talk, she is the worst. Like, she's dumb as a rock, she smells like a truck stop bathroom, and she once tried to microwave a whole chicken still in the package.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: But seriously, thank you. You're a good dude.

jokes.text: Yeah, but does it have to be this family?
jokes.setup: Ben says 'got to keep it in the family' about hiring Mona-Lisa
jokes.punchline: Tom's weary response signals he already regrets the decision
jokes.explanation: A compact, efficient reaction beat. Works as a quick laugh on the heels of the bigger Jean-Ralphio moment. Nothing groundbreaking but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: You can't leave early. We have a strict policy.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're not gonna let me go? Fine. I'm gonna burn this place down.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa, you can't threaten arson.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa Saperstein
dialogue.line: I'm not threatening it. I'm promising it.

jokes.text: I need to leave early today because my shrink got me and him tickets to a Pitbull concert. And I already committed to that. And so if you say that I can't go, it's like you're taking something away from me.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa asks to leave the store early on her first day
jokes.punchline: Her excuse involves her therapist taking her to a Pitbull concert, framed as a therapeutic commitment — and she pre-frames any denial as an act of emotional violence
jokes.explanation: Brilliant layering: the therapist attending a Pitbull concert is absurd, her reframing Tom's refusal as emotional harm is a perfect manipulation tactic. It works on multiple levels — absurdist premise plus character-specific narcissistic logic. Mona-Lisa's manipulative reasoning is a great comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: She's gonna get her way, she's gonna get her way, she always gets her way. Oh, why do I even try? I know that she's gonna get her way.

jokes.text: Um, I totally hear you. Um, I also don't like what you're saying. So if you say no, I will start a fire in the bathroom.
jokes.setup: Tom says the store is busy and he needs her to stay
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's 'negotiation' escalates from passive acknowledgment to arson threat without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: Among the best jokes in the episode. The structure is flawless: 'I hear you / I don't like what you're saying / arson.' Each beat escalates perfectly. The arson threat is so specific and matter-of-fact that it's genuinely shocking. This is the Mona-Lisa joke that defines her character. Extremely quotable. Comparable to a strong 8+ anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, if you want something more upbeat than Paths of Glory, how about a 9-hour Holocaust documentary?

jokes.text: Okay, I guess you can go. / Yeah, I know I can.
jokes.setup: Tom caves to Mona-Lisa's arson threat and grants her permission to leave
jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa doesn't even acknowledge it as permission — she states she was going regardless
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the arson bit. Tom's capitulation is funny, but Mona-Lisa dismissing even his surrender as irrelevant is the real punchline. Establishes her worldview completely: his authority was never real to her.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is a beloved classic, but let's be honest — completely unrealistic. A alien shows up in a California suburb, befriends a ten-year-old boy, and nobody calls the government? Please. I'm giving E.T. one star.

jokes.text: Today we'll be screening Stanley Kubrick's 1957 classic Paths Of Glory. It's about three men who refuse to go on a suicide mission and are executed for cowardice. Or we could, you know, maybe screen a different movie. One that's a little bit more upbeat. Like Finding Nemo or... / I could do, uh, Shoah.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests something more upbeat than Paths of Glory
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers Shoah — a 9-hour documentary about the Holocaust — as an 'upbeat' alternative
jokes.explanation: The joke works beautifully because Dennis is completely sincere — 'Shoah' as a counterproposal to Finding Nemo reveals his total blind spot to what 'upbeat' means. It also lands as a slightly dark film-nerd joke that the comedy-savvy audience will appreciate doubly. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Where am I? What year is it? Did I just see a movie or did I have a stroke?

jokes.text: This is the place where Perd Hapley shot his movie review show Lights, Camera, Perd. It's a heartwarming story, but it's just not believable. Which is why I give E.T. 1 1/2 stars.
jokes.setup: Leslie is enthusiastically describing the cultural value of Pawnee Videodome
jokes.punchline: She reveals Perd Hapley gave E.T. 1.5 stars because it's 'not believable' — a perfect joke about Perd's literal-mindedness
jokes.explanation: A tidy multi-character joke: it's funny about Perd (the recurring anchor-who-states-the-obvious) AND funny that Leslie includes this anecdote as part of a sincere endorsement of the store. Perd's literal-minded dismissal of E.T.'s believability is the specific detail that makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Would you be interested in renting a movie from us?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: No thanks, I'm actually illegally streaming everything at home.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh... well, I'm a government official, so...

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Right, I probably shouldn't have said that.

jokes.text: Andy, it's over. Get up, Andy. What are you doing? / What's everybody-- where are we?
jokes.setup: The group is watching Paths of Glory at the Videodome
jokes.punchline: Andy has apparently been so absorbed (or asleep) in the depressing film that he's disoriented when it ends
jokes.explanation: A reliable Andy beat — his childlike confusion is always charming. Not especially novel but fits the character and setting well. The disorientation gag works quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want to rent Finding Nemo.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How about instead you rent 'Finding Nemo's Remains: A Deep Sea Tragedy'? It's a depressing documentary about fish extinction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That sounds horrible.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The tagline is 'He wasn't lost. He was dead the whole time.' We call it 'Finding Nemesis.'

jokes.text: The reason I love that film is that it's really depressing.
jokes.setup: Dennis gives his endorsement of Paths of Glory
jokes.punchline: He cites its depression as its primary virtue, matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: A clean Dennis character beat delivered with perfect economy. His aesthetic worldview (depression = value) is established in six words. It's funny because there's no irony in it — he means it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just want some normal Red Vines. You know, classic American candy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sorry, we're all out. But I've got some great options. How about these Norwegian licorice whips? Or these Japanese pork-flavored gummies?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pork-flavored? Dennis, these are insane.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's also this Lithuanian beet candy and some Thai fish-paste lozengers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How is this what we have?

jokes.text: Why would I do that? All movies are online for free. I'm watching Iron Man 2 on my phone right now.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks a man in the store to rent something to support Dennis's business
jokes.punchline: He's already watching a movie on his phone inside the video store — the embodiment of why video stores are dying
jokes.explanation: Great observational/situational joke — the irony of streaming a movie on your phone inside a dying video store is sharp and the specific choice of Iron Man 2 (not even a prestige film) adds texture. A good 'Pawnee citizen as comedic foil' moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Families are really important to people.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: I, for one, am going to rent Finding Nemo. / Ooh, we don't carry cartoons. But if you want a film about the ocean, we have a documentary about the brutality of Japan's whaling industry. It's called Tears Of My Blowhole. And it's--it's nauseating.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to be positive and rent a cheerful film
jokes.punchline: Dennis steers her toward 'Tears of My Blowhole,' a nauseating whale documentary — his depressing alternative to every cheerful suggestion
jokes.explanation: The title 'Tears of My Blowhole' alone is exceptional — it's a made-up documentary title that sounds exactly like something this character would stock and recommend. It extends the Shoah joke's logic into a running character gag (Dennis always escalates toward the bleakest option). The title has become a fan-favorite quotable moment from this episode. High craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Have you made your decision?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm 60% sure I want to do it, but I'm also 70% sure I don't want to do it.

jokes.text: I'll just buy some red vines. / Oh, we only have Japanese slime candy and, um, Bulgarian wheat balls.
jokes.setup: Leslie falls back to buying snacks when she can't rent anything
jokes.punchline: Dennis doesn't carry normal candy — only inexplicably specific foreign snacks that sound deeply unpleasant
jokes.explanation: 'Bulgarian wheat balls' is a perfectly constructed fake-unpleasant food. The specificity of nationality and texture is what makes it funny. Extends Dennis's character joke naturally — of course he doesn't stock Red Vines. Quick and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You should practice on Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He's basically a baby anyway.

jokes.text: Leslie, seriously, where are we?
jokes.setup: The group is trying to help a failing video store
jokes.punchline: Andy is still disoriented from the film — he has genuinely lost track of where he is in real space
jokes.explanation: A callback to the earlier Andy beat. Works as a running Andy confusion gag but the repetition slightly diminishes it. Still charming, consistent with character.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Is Mona-Lisa stealing from us?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah, she's a kleptomaniac, a nymphomaniac, and a pyromaniac.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's three different things.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I know. She's got a lot going on.

jokes.text: All these kids have fathers and mothers who have birthed them and are guiding them through life. / Yep, that's how it works.
jokes.setup: Chris is staring at children in the store while wrestling with Ann's sperm donation request
jokes.punchline: Ben's completely straight acknowledgment of Chris's obvious observation is the joke — the gap between Chris's existential spiral and Ben's total indifference
jokes.explanation: A very Parks-specific joke: Ben's deadpan validation of the completely obvious is perfectly timed. Chris's awed observation about basic human biology as if seeing it for the first time is a great character beat — his optimism taken to its absurd extreme.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We could use Tom as a practice baby.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that is the most brilliant, innovative, forward-thinking idea anyone has ever had in the entire history of human civilization. You should be awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. We should name a city after you. Future generations will study your genius in schools. You've basically solved all of humanity's problems with that one sentence.

jokes.text: How are you feeling? Did you make your dad-cision yet?
jokes.setup: Ben asks Chris about whether he's decided to donate sperm
jokes.punchline: 'Dad-cision' — a portmanteau that Ben delivers with zero fanfare
jokes.explanation: A clean wordplay beat. 'Dad-cision' is a functional pun delivered matter-of-factly by Ben, which is in character. Not a classic, but it gets a quick laugh and moves the story forward.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Wait, you guys are making fake babies? Dude, I'm in. I thought you said fake drugs.

jokes.text: I am 100% certain that I am 0% sure of what I'm going to do.
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Chris has made his decision about donating sperm
jokes.punchline: Chris's pseudo-confident response is a mathematical contradiction wrapped in his signature positivity-speak
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Chris's brand of self-help speak is perfectly lampooned — he sounds decisive and positive while saying literally nothing. '100% certain that I am 0% sure' is a mathematically precise way to say 'no idea' and only Chris would phrase his uncertainty in confidence metrics. Highly quotable and very strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you tell anyone about this, I will actually kill you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: About what? That you've been volunteering at the animal shelter on weekends?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes. Now you're dead.

jokes.text: It's a battle between my primal desire to bring a child into this world and my paralyzing fear of negatively affecting any living thing.
jokes.setup: Chris explains his internal conflict about the sperm donation (talking head)
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition: 'primal desire' vs 'paralyzing fear of negatively affecting any living thing' — the second half undercuts the heroic first half completely
jokes.explanation: Good talking-head joke about Chris's hyper-aware self-analysis. The oversharing mixed with comedic self-deprecation ('negatively affecting any living thing') is perfectly Chris. Works as character comedy and mild cringe.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I need you to write me a recommendation letter.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Of course! For what?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My job application to be a professional horse whisperer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: April, you work in the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know. Just tell them about my experience as a veterinary surgeon.

jokes.text: There's $60 missing from the register. I think Mona-Lisa's stealing from me. / Yeah, it is absolutely Mona-Lisa. 100%. She's a total klepto. And nympho and pyro-- all those things.
jokes.setup: Tom suspects Mona-Lisa of theft
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately confirms it and lists her other '-o' disorders with cheerful authority: klepto, nympho, pyro — 'all those things'
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's list of Mona-Lisa's disorders is excellent — the escalation through the '-o' suffix words and the breezy 'all those things' as a catch-all is perfectly constructed. The fact that he knows these things and still recommended her for the job is the implicit joke. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know the vet through hookups, right?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No! What? No.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: ...Okay, yes.

jokes.text: You know, when I was in high school, we had to spend a week carrying around a sack of flour, pretending it was a kid. Why don't you make Tom your sack of flour, see how it feels to parent him a little?
jokes.setup: Ann is advising Ben on how to handle Tom and Mona-Lisa
jokes.punchline: She applies the high school 'flour sack baby' assignment to Tom Haverford as a literal life coaching method
jokes.explanation: Funny in concept — treating a grown man like a flour-sack baby — but slightly underdeveloped. The joke is mostly in the premise and payoff elsewhere. Works as setup for the 'sack of flour' B-plot thread.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying we have to be friends?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, yes. That's what coworkers do.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ugh. This is worse than slavery.

jokes.text: Ben, that is literally the greatest idea in human history.
jokes.setup: Ben relays Ann's 'flour sack' idea to Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom's hyperbolic endorsement of what is a mildly useful but completely ordinary idea
jokes.explanation: Tom's hyperbole is a recurring character beat that works okay here but isn't especially fresh. It's a functional laugh but relies on a familiar Tom tic rather than a specific joke construction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So you're saying you've slept with the vet?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No! I don't just sleep with every person I meet.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But you've slept with this vet.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes.

jokes.text: I heard 'sack of flour' and 'high school.' Are you dingdongs making fake drugs for sophomores? Because if true, this guy wants in.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio overhears fragments of Ann and Ben's conversation
jokes.punchline: His interpretation — fake drugs for high schoolers — is a non-sequitur that reveals exactly how his brain works, and he immediately volunteers
jokes.explanation: A great Jean-Ralphio non-sequitur. 'Dingdongs' as an insult, the criminal misinterpretation, and 'this guy wants in' all feel authentically Jean-Ralphio. The joke reveals his character while being genuinely surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have something to say. *slams hand on table* We need to cut the budget by 40%. We will lose 200 jobs. The Parks Department will be gutted. *slams hand again* This is a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: See? Ron, you're doing it!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Doing what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Slam poetry! You made it sound powerful!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wasn't doing slam poetry. I was just talking about something important. If I said the same thing like this — *speaks monotone* 'we need to cut the budget by 40%, we will lose 200 jobs' — it's the same information. The slam poetry doesn't change the content. It's just... noise.

jokes.text: Generally, between us, April always has the upper hand. And that hand is usually giving me the finger or pouring honey in my purse. But now I have the upper hand. And I'm going to use it to crush her... Into being nice to me.
jokes.setup: Ann describes her power dynamic with April in a talking head
jokes.punchline: The 'crush her' setup implies revenge; the punchline reveals the crushing is into friendship
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed misdirection. 'Pouring honey in my purse' is an inspired and specific piece of April cruelty. The beat where Ann pauses before '...Into being nice to me' is a perfect structural pivot. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Dennis, you are a blight upon this earth. Your incompetence knows no bounds. You waddle through life like a penguin with a drinking problem, leaving destruction in your wake.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your voice is like a thousand dying cats. Your face, a monument to poor life choices. And your haircut—dear God, your haircut is a cry for help that no one will answer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You are the human equivalent of a participation trophy. Useless. Unwanted. A constant reminder of society's failures.

jokes.text: So I really need a letter of recommendation. And since you work in a hospital, as a janitor... / Nurse.
jokes.setup: April needs Ann's help and is trying to frame the ask as a favor to someone less important
jokes.punchline: She deliberately misidentifies Ann as a janitor; Ann's single-word correction is perfectly deadpan
jokes.explanation: Economy is nearly perfect — the entire joke is one word ('Nurse.'). April's condescension and Ann's resigned correction capture their relationship in six total words. Classic Parks economy of dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa scares me because she physically assaulted a police horse.

jokes.text: Because you hooked up with him? / I don't hook up with everyone I know. Although, yes, we did hook up.
jokes.setup: Ann says she knows the veterinary school director; April immediately assumes it's from a hookup
jokes.punchline: Ann protests she doesn't hook up with everyone — then immediately confirms this was a hookup
jokes.explanation: A tight little three-beat joke: April's correct assumption → Ann's denial → immediate self-contradiction. The structure is clean and Ann's self-awareness makes it funnier than a simple 'yes.' A recurring Parks joke about Ann's romantic history done well.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to stand up for yourself more. You're a capable guy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You've got... you've got a really solid midsection. I mean that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ben.

jokes.text: No, you have to be my friend. / No, that is so much worse.
jokes.setup: April assumes Ann's condition for the letter will be servitude
jokes.punchline: Ann demands friendship instead — which April finds far more horrifying than slavery
jokes.explanation: A highlight of the episode. April's horrified 'that is so much worse' captures her character perfectly and is also a sharp structural reversal — the 'worse than slavery' implication is darkly funny. Maximum economy, excellent character specificity. Both characters are essential to this joke; it couldn't land without both of them.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I know Mona-Lisa's been spreading rumors about me, but I'm not comfortable confronting her. She's... intimidating.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: If anything happens to me, I just want you to know: please delete my browser history.

jokes.text: Anything can be a slam poem if you say it like this. / It's pointless. / This man is a failure. / He is not up to snuff. / His business is failing, and you're bailing it out.
jokes.setup: Ron dismisses slam poetry as intellectual-gathering because the poems don't rhyme
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates what a slam poem sounds like by delivering his criticism of the bailout AS a slam poem — turning his own argument into the thing he's mocking
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. Ron Swanson unwittingly demonstrating slam poetry while simultaneously mocking it is excellent structural comedy — he proves the point he's trying to refute. The irony is perfect and the joke is completely rooted in his character (libertarian, anti-arts-funding, literal). High craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You want the government to bail out these failing businesses? That's like asking a hunter to shoot a deer in the face because it's having trouble finding food. It's not mercy, it's weakness. And then you'd have venison all over city hall.

jokes.text: Get popular films that people wanna see. Like, uh, get the Tarkovsky movies with the subtitles. / No. Like Pixar. Reese Witherspoon. I know this is gonna hurt, but maybe some Michael Bay. / What? No, no. No.
jokes.setup: Leslie advises Dennis to stock popular films to save his business
jokes.punchline: Her idea of 'popular' starts with Andrei Tarkovsky (famously inaccessible arthouse filmmaker); Dennis recoils at Michael Bay the way most people recoil at something vile
jokes.explanation: The Tarkovsky detail is the key — Leslie thinks she's making a concession to popularity and leads with one of cinema's most austere directors. Dennis's physical 'No, no, no' at Michael Bay is the comedic flip: to him, Michael Bay is the holocaust of cinema. Well-executed double character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to need you to stop making hunting metaphors about women.

jokes.text: Tom, I have something I need to talk to you about. / Do we need to sit like this? / Yes.
jokes.setup: Ben wants to have a serious conversation with Tom
jokes.punchline: They are apparently seated in some formal or awkward configuration that Tom questions; Ben insisting on maintaining it implies the visual is worth the laugh
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual gag (we see the seating arrangement on screen) that works better with the visual than it reads in transcript. Ben insisting on the format while having a 'dad talk' with Tom is a good character beat — Ben leaning into the flour-sack parenting concept.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've never actually seen Rashomon, but I love that it exists.

jokes.text: She scares the crap out of me. I once saw her punch a police horse in the face.
jokes.setup: Ben tells Tom to stand up to Mona-Lisa
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals his real issue: he saw her assault a police horse. This is his evidence that she is dangerous.
jokes.explanation: A standout joke. 'Punch a police horse in the face' is an inspired piece of violence — the specificity (not just a horse, a POLICE horse; not just hit it, PUNCHED IT IN THE FACE) makes it hilarious. It perfectly establishes Mona-Lisa's dangerous unpredictability through one vivid image. Highly quotable, great economy, excellent character reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa, I'm not going to let you treat me like this anymore. I deserve respect.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Oh wow. That's actually really hot. I'm getting wet right now.

jokes.text: You're Tom Haverford. You're a smart, successful young man with an adorable, little belly.
jokes.setup: Ben gives Tom a pep talk
jokes.punchline: The encouragement is undercut by 'adorable, little belly' — a gentle insult delivered as if it's a compliment
jokes.explanation: A small but well-landed joke. Ben's earnestness makes the 'adorable little belly' detail funnier — he means it as genuine encouragement. The specificity of the physical detail elevates it beyond a generic pep-talk joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want a guy who's really into cooking, but also a vegetarian, but also loves steak. Someone who's really smart, but also really dumb. A guy who's really tall, but also really short. Someone who's really rich, but also completely broke. A guy who's really handsome, but also really ugly. Someone who's really confident, but also has severe anxiety. A guy who's really outgoing, but also a total introvert.

jokes.text: And if she murders me, tell Jean-Ralphio to clear my browser history.
jokes.setup: Tom agrees to confront Mona-Lisa
jokes.punchline: He treats murder as a likely outcome and his primary concern is the browser history — not a goodbye to loved ones
jokes.explanation: Great Tom joke — the browser history gag is timeless and the specificity of going to Jean-Ralphio (his ride-or-die) makes it character-specific. The dark premise (murder as a real possibility) is funny because of how casual Tom is about it. Well-earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm like fracking for friendship. I keep drilling and drilling until I hit something.

jokes.text: Thanks for the advice, man. / You're welcome. / Son. / What's that? / Nothing.
jokes.setup: Ben has been playing 'father figure' to Tom per Ann's flour-sack advice
jokes.punchline: He accidentally calls Tom 'son,' then immediately retreats when Tom notices
jokes.explanation: A small but well-timed bit that pays off the 'parent Tom' setup. Ben's 'Nothing' is perfectly embarrassed. The whole exchange in about six words. Economical callback to the flour-sack premise.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't understand why the government insists on handing out food stamps and welfare to people who won't work. It's a disgrace.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, food stamps and welfare ARE government help.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Yes, well... that's different.

jokes.text: Pawnee Videodome is where I rented my first Bruce Lee movie. And my second Bruce Lee movie. And when I was in seventh grade, I went out back in the alley behind the store, and there was a giant hornet's nest. And I threw a rock at it, and it exploded. And hornets came out. Andy- / The point is, obviously, you do not throw rocks at a hornet's nest.
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing meaningful memories of Pawnee Videodome to make a case for saving it
jokes.punchline: Andy's contribution escalates from Bruce Lee nostalgia to an inexplicable hornet attack story, then he draws a lesson completely unrelated to saving the store
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy storytelling: what starts as a sentimental memory derails into chaos and ends with an unrelated moral. The two Bruce Lee movies as separate milestones, the hornet's nest, and 'obviously, you do not throw rocks at a hornet's nest' as his contribution to a policy debate is perfectly Andy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It immediately turned into sex and a relationship

jokes.text: And the point is also that the Pawnee Videodome is a place with tremendous community value.
jokes.setup: Andy has just concluded his hornet-nest digression
jokes.punchline: He pivots back to the point as if the hornet story was a normal supporting argument
jokes.explanation: A button to Andy's story — the return to 'community value' after the hornet digression. Works as an extension of the previous joke rather than a standalone moment. Consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Tom, I need to borrow some money.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mona-Lisa, that's none of your beeswax.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm thinking about getting into the bee waxing business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, so it IS your beeswax?

jokes.text: What are you doing at a city council meeting? Are you lost? Are you hurt?
jokes.setup: Ron Swanson appears at a city council meeting to oppose the Videodome bailout
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine concern that he might be physically lost or injured — the idea of Ron voluntarily attending government proceedings is so out of character it reads as an emergency
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke rooted in years of character consistency — Ron's anti-government philosophy is so established that his voluntary appearance at a government meeting is inherently absurd. Leslie's maternal concern (is he lost? is he hurt?) is the perfect reaction. Strong character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Yo, Tom, I need to borrow some money.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why should I lend you money?

dialogue.speaker: Mona-Lisa
dialogue.line: Because it's none of your beeswax.

jokes.text: The government should not prop up a failed business. That would be like giving food to a mortally wounded animal instead of slitting its throat and properly utilizing its meat and pelt.
jokes.setup: Ron argues against the government bailout of Pawnee Videodome
jokes.punchline: His analogy for economic compassion is throat-slitting and pelt-utilization — delivered as a completely reasonable comparison
jokes.explanation: A top-tier Ron Swanson joke. The logic is airtight within Ron's worldview: why prolong suffering when you can efficiently harvest the animal? Applying this to economic policy is darkly funny and brilliantly in character. 'Properly utilizing its meat and pelt' is the detail that elevates it — he's thought this through. Comparable to the 8+ anchor. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Just pick something, April.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I can't think. Your hair is distracting me. It looks like a llama died on your head.

jokes.text: Please stop talking about wounded meat.
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered his 'slit the throat and use the pelt' analogy
jokes.punchline: Leslie's exasperated plea reduces Ron's entire libertarian economic philosophy to 'wounded meat'
jokes.explanation: A perfect button. Five words that reduce Ron's philosophical argument to its most absurd literal element. The phrase 'wounded meat' is oddly specific and funny. Leslie's weariness is completely earned. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh, I'll just go. Ann and I are best friends now. Temporarily.

jokes.text: You rented Rashomon? What was your favorite part of that? / I haven't rented it, actually, yet. But I like the idea that there is a place where I could rent Rashomon.
jokes.setup: Leslie advocates for the Videodome as a place where people can rent films like Rashomon
jokes.punchline: She's never actually rented it — she just likes the concept of its availability existing
jokes.explanation: A quietly brilliant joke about cultural aspiration vs. actual engagement. Leslie's whole argument for the Videodome collapses: she's fighting to preserve something she's never actually used in the way she claims. 'I like the idea that there is a place where I could rent Rashomon' is an exceptionally well-observed line about civic pride and highbrow posturing. Strong character integration — this is very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We could braid each other's hair and talk about boys we like.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Or we could paint our nails and stay up until like, 9 PM talking about our feelings.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Or we could just sit in a circle and judge other girls. That's what friends do, right?

jokes.text: Uh, you can just watch it online, for free, whenever you want. / Bailiff!
jokes.setup: Leslie's position is undermined by Ron pointing out Rashomon is online for free
jokes.punchline: Leslie calls for the bailiff to remove Ron rather than respond to his factually correct point
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. Leslie uses governmental authority to escape an argument she can't win. 'Bailiff!' as a response to a factual observation is a perfect abuse of institutional power for comedic ends. Very in-character for Leslie in council mode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Government has no business telling people what they can and cannot watch in the privacy of their own homes. But apparently, it has every business turning a beloved video rental establishment into a den of pornography.

jokes.text: Thank you, Mr. Swanson, for your absurd opinion, which is shared by no one.
jokes.setup: Leslie officially dismisses Ron's public comment at the council meeting
jokes.punchline: She thanks him in formal council language while calling his opinion absurd in the same breath
jokes.explanation: A decent Leslie-in-council-mode joke. The formal courtesy of 'thank you' followed by 'absurd opinion, which is shared by no one' is good but not exceptional. Well-delivered in tone and rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? The video store is a front for a porn operation?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Apparently.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And the city has been unknowingly complicit in this? Oh my God, we need to shut this down immediately. This is a disaster. A pornographic disaster.

jokes.text: How much to rent this jacket? / Oh. Curly Sue, that jacket is so ugly. You should just take it. / It's 15 for the day, 40 for the week. / Thank you. / We appreciate your business.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is supposed to be at the Pitbull concert but appears at the city council meeting — and tries to rent a jacket during formal proceedings
jokes.punchline: Tom insults the jacket while still completing the transaction; 'We appreciate your business' in the middle of a council meeting
jokes.explanation: Funny situational absurdism — a Rent-A-Swag transaction happening during a city council meeting. Tom calling the jacket ugly while selling it is a nice Tom-ism. 'We appreciate your business' as formal council-session dialogue works well.

dialogue.speaker: Brandi Maxxxx
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for supporting my work, Leslie. It really means a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Of course! I'm always here for you.

dialogue.speaker: Brandi Maxxxx
dialogue.line: In fact, I was so inspired by your support that I made a porn about this exact situation.

jokes.text: Did I order the what for the what-what what, what?
jokes.setup: Tom asks if Mona-Lisa ordered champagne for the client party
jokes.punchline: Her response is a cascade of 'whats' that communicates genuine bafflement at the concept of work
jokes.explanation: A great Mona-Lisa line — her non-comprehension of basic professional responsibilities expressed as a verbal meltdown of 'whats' is perfectly in character. The repetition pattern is funny and feels authentic to how this character talks.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That didn't mean anything. We're not friends. Don't tell anyone about this.

jokes.text: Okay, sure, but after I take a quick nap because ecstasy takes ♪ forever to leave my system.
jokes.setup: Tom demands they discuss her work habits now
jokes.punchline: She mentions being on ecstasy as casually as someone might mention a headache, and sings 'forever' with a little melody
jokes.explanation: Mona-Lisa's drug use as a casual impediment to work is darkly funny. The musical delivery of 'forever' (the same tic as Jean-Ralphio) is great — it's a family trait. Strong character specificity and the matter-of-fact confession is perfectly in her register.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom is like flour. He starts out as nothing, and then with the right environment and some heat, he becomes bread.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's actually really nice, man.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But then he becomes a bran muffin, which is the peak of flour achievement.

jokes.text: You are so freaking sexy right now, I could crap my pants.
jokes.setup: Tom threatens to fire Mona-Lisa if she doesn't shape up
jokes.punchline: She finds his authority so attractive that she responds with sexual arousal described in deeply unromantic terms
jokes.explanation: A perfect Mona-Lisa joke — she's so unpredictable that even a firing threat becomes flirtation. The specific crudeness of 'I could crap my pants' as a romantic expression is inspired and deeply character-specific. It also completely disarms Tom's attempt at authority. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, being a parent is all about being present and listening to your kids. Really hearing what they have to say, you know? It's about creating a safe space where they feel valued and—wait, am I allowed to keep talking? Because I have so much more. Did you know that consistency is key? And also snacks. Kids need snacks. But like, healthy snacks. Or just snacks. Any snacks really. And you gotta be patient, super patient, because kids are basically tiny drunk people who can't operate doors, and—oh man, I'm on a roll here—you should definitely read to them, but not like boring books, fun books with pictures, or maybe audiobooks while you're driving, which is actually genius when you think about it, and oh! Make sure they know you love them every single day, multiple times a day, maybe tattoo it on your forehead so they see it when they wake up, and also establish boundaries, but like, fun boundaries, and—I'm sorry, what was the question?

jokes.text: I guess it would have to be Channing Tatum's body, Ryan Gosling's face, and Michael Fassbender's... sense of humor. / What about you? / Yao Ming's torso, Napoleon's brain, and The Hunchback of Notre Dame's hunchback.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa and April are playing 'build your perfect guy'
jokes.punchline: April's ideal man includes Napoleon's brain (concerning) and the Hunchback's hunchback — the hunchback being a selling point, not a flaw
jokes.explanation: Excellent April character joke. Mona-Lisa's answer is funny (the Fassbender/sense of humor bit is a good subversion), but April's answer is the real punchline — the Hunchback's hunchback as a desired physical feature is bizarre and perfect. Napoleon's brain signals attraction to a megalomaniacal conqueror. This is April distilled into a dating game. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I can eat twelve people.

jokes.text: Even though she hides it underneath layers of sarcasm, resentment, and grumpiness, I know, deep down somewhere, April likes me. I'm kind of just fracking for friendship.
jokes.setup: Ann talks head about her forced friendship experiment with April
jokes.punchline: 'Fracking for friendship' — the industrial mining metaphor for excavating warmth from April
jokes.explanation: 'Fracking for friendship' is a genuinely clever metaphor — the environmental damage/effort to extract something valuable (friendship from April) lands as an original construction. The setup with 'layers of sarcasm, resentment, and grumpiness' is also good character description. A strong talking-head joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't need utensils. I have no use for them.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Food is already in its simplest form. Eating it with instruments is over-complicating things.

jokes.text: I heard you were giving out free money. I need $3,000. Minimum.
jokes.setup: Leslie is fielding public comments at the city council meeting about the Videodome
jokes.punchline: A random citizen walks in demanding a personal loan from the city government, and specifies a minimum
jokes.explanation: A solid 'Pawnee citizen as absurd interruption' joke. The 'minimum' qualifier is good — it suggests he's thought about negotiating. Works as a quick gag in the escalating series of council interruptions.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I got you something. It's practical and useful, which is why I'm giving it to you instead of keeping it for myself. I don't do gifts well, but you're my best friend, so I'm making an exception. Don't make this weird by getting emotional about it.

jokes.text: What would you do if one of your citizens was about to come into some serious physical harm... Unless he got $3,000? / I'd call the police. / You cannot call the police.
jokes.setup: The citizen is trying to threaten Leslie into giving him money
jokes.punchline: His 'threat' is so poorly constructed that Leslie immediately calls his bluff; his panicked 'you cannot call the police' reveals it as self-directed harm extortion
jokes.explanation: A good escalation from the previous joke — the man's threat is clumsy, his 'you cannot call the police' is the reveal that he was threatening to harm himself. Funny as a dark absurdist beat, though the character isn't developed enough for full impact.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm happy to help you and Ben with this. It's a beautiful thing you're doing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thank you so much, Chris. We really appreciate it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what they say - this is really going to be a womb with a view.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I mean, we're going to have such a strong cervix- I mean, service. Partnership. We're really going to... uterus well together.

jokes.text: Wilson Gromling of the 'Liberty or Die' party. These government handouts are deplorable. I was on food stamps. I was on Welfare. And nobody ever helped me.
jokes.setup: A libertarian citizen testifies against the government giving any handouts
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he was on food stamps and welfare — undermining his own argument in real time with no apparent awareness
jokes.explanation: A sharp political joke delivered economically. The logical contradiction (I hate government help / the government helped me) is well-set up and lands with good irony. 'Nobody ever helped me' after listing two forms of government assistance is the punchline — his total lack of self-awareness is the joke. Relevant and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What is this? This isn't The Sound of Music!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It appears to be a pornographic parody.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at these character names. 'Porn Leslie'? 'Porn Ron'? This is ridiculous!

jokes.text: The Pawnee chapter of the 'Liberty or Die' party has hit some hard times. We were wondering if maybe the town could loan us some money.
jokes.setup: The same anti-bailout libertarian who just testified against government handouts
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks for a government loan for his anti-government-handout political party
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback that perfectly completes the Wilson Gromling joke. The hypocrisy loop is closed: he opposes handouts, revealed he benefited from them, and now actively requests one. The 'Liberty or Die' party asking for a loan is a devastating irony that the show earns by setting it up properly. The escalation from Joke 52 to this is well-structured.

jokes.text: Tom, how did it go with Mona-Lisa? / I told her she needed to change her attitude, or I was gonna have to fire her. / Well, that is very responsible and mature. She took it well? / Um... yeah. / For some reason, she got super turned on. We started making out. Hard. Next thing you know, we're back at my place, having sex. We're together now.
jokes.setup: Ben asks if Tom's confrontation went well; Tom confirms it did
jokes.punchline: The reality: his authority display turned into a hookup and they're now in a relationship — he completely failed to address the work problem
jokes.explanation: A great structural payoff: we saw Mona-Lisa get turned on by Tom's authority, and now we get the full aftermath. 'We started making out. Hard.' as an aside, then 'We're together now' delivered as a status update is excellent escalation. Tom's complete capitulation to Mona-Lisa even while 'winning' is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head about Mona-Lisa: 'Um...yeah. For some reason, she got super turned on. We started making out. Hard. Next thing you know, we're back at my place, having sex. We're together now.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom if he talked to Mona-Lisa and how she took it.
jokes.punchline: The euphemistic build — 'for some reason,' 'making out, hard,' 'back at my place' — culminating in the matter-of-fact 'We're together now.' Tom has completely abandoned the parenting experiment in favor of dating the chaos.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire Mona-Lisa arc's first act. Tom's helpless surrender is funnier for being presented so casually. 'Making out. Hard.' as a standalone sentence is a great comedic pause. The 'we're together now' as the logical endpoint of a confrontation-gone-wrong is very Tom.

jokes.text: Hey, bitch, I need to borrow some money to do something that is none of your damn beeswax, namely, I need to wax my bee.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa approaches as Tom's new girlfriend at the party
jokes.punchline: She opens with 'bitch,' says her need is 'none of your beeswax,' then immediately reveals it's literal waxing — the wordplay accidentally self-undermines her own rudeness
jokes.explanation: Excellent Mona-Lisa construction — 'none of your beeswax, namely, I need to wax my bee' is a perfect inadvertent pun that she delivers without any awareness. Her rudeness ('bitch') combined with her accidental wordplay is quintessential Mona-Lisa: simultaneously terrible and unintentionally funny.

jokes.text: Here you go. / I'd still hit it. / I'm coolin' on you.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa borrows money and leaves; Jean-Ralphio expresses attraction to his own sister
jokes.punchline: Tom shuts him down — 'I'm coolin' on you' — a gentle but decisive relationship demotion
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio expressing sexual interest in his twin sister is darkly absurdist — the show keeps it brief so it doesn't overstay. Tom's 'coolin' on you' is a nicely understated relationship consequence. Works as a quick dark beat.

jokes.text: What about you? Build your perfect guy. Um... Yao Ming's torso, Napoleon's brain, and The Hunchback of Notre Dame's hunchback. [Ann reacts to April's hunchback answer]
jokes.setup: April delivers her 'perfect guy' answer ending with the Hunchback's hunchback
jokes.punchline: Ann's visible bewilderment/discomfort at the hunchback being a positive physical attribute
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat from Ann extends the April joke. Ann's genuine confusion at April's preferences is the straight-man moment that gives the April joke space to land. Separately it's a 7, but it's really part of the same comedic unit as Joke 48.

jokes.text: Back to forced friendship. Hey, let's go put on our pj's and make White Russians. So fun.
jokes.setup: Chris gives up trying to talk to Ann privately and leaves.
jokes.punchline: April pivots immediately from aggressive interference to chirpy forced-friendship activities, delivered with maximum deadpan insincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Back to forced friendship' as a literal verbal bookmark is a great line — April narrates her own insincerity. The pivot to White Russians delivered with zero warmth is perfect deadpan. 'So fun.' as its own sentence with no inflection is the button.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, this is amazing, Dennis. / Hey. / You did it! / We did it! I did it. / Yes, it was.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives to see the 'improved' Videodome
jokes.punchline: Dennis's swift 'We did it! I did it' correction is a confident attribution shift — he takes sole credit mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: A quick but effective character beat — Dennis's pivot from 'we' to 'I' mid-sentence is quietly funny and consistent with the self-absorbed art house persona.

jokes.text: I took your advice. Got rid of all those dusty, old foreign films and used the money for the part of our business that's always done pretty well for us. / Give the people what they want, right? / This isn't what people want. / It's definitely what that guy wants. / I like this store now.
jokes.setup: Leslie expects to see a mainstream-film-stocking Videodome; the reveal is that Dennis converted to porn
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'It's definitely what that guy wants' (pointing to a customer) and 'I like this store now' are the perfect libertarian endorsement of a porn shop
jokes.explanation: The episode's main reveal joke. The structure is very strong — Dennis's pivot to porn is unexpected, and Ron's immediate approval ('I like this store now') is a perfect payoff that vindicates his free-market philosophy while undermining Leslie's good intentions. Ron's 'It's definitely what that guy wants' is precision-aimed and completely in character.

jokes.text: Do you realize what you have done? The Pawnee government now effectively owns a porn shop. You have made us porn peddlers!
jokes.setup: Leslie reacts to the Videodome's transformation into an adult video store
jokes.punchline: 'Porn peddlers!' — her complete horror, expressed in the language of Victorian moral outrage
jokes.explanation: Leslie's outrage is well-performed and 'porn peddlers' is a satisfying phrase. The word choice reveals her character — she talks like a 1950s civic reformer. Works as a good reaction beat following the reveal.

jokes.text: Hello everyone, I'm Brandi Maxxxx. Let's give a big round of applause to Councilwoman Knope for keeping this store in business! / No. Everyone stop applauding.
jokes.setup: A porn actress appears at the newly converted store's reopening
jokes.punchline: She publicly credits Leslie — forcing Leslie to desperately distance herself while surrounded by applause she can't stop
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-comedy setup. Leslie's 'No. Everyone stop applauding' in response to being thanked by a porn actress is the right reaction and delivered in character. Brandi Maxxxx as a recurring Parks character always lands due to the contrast with Leslie's civic earnestness.

jokes.text: Leslie, you've always been a huge supporter of my work. / No, no, I haven't. / So I'm thrilled to tell you that I'm playing Leslie Knope in the porn version of the story of this government bailout! / Please don't do that. / Oh, we already filmed it. / Oh!
jokes.setup: Brandi Maxxxx enthusiastically tells Leslie about her role in an adult film
jokes.punchline: A porn parody of Leslie's government bailout already exists — the escalation 'Oh, we already filmed it' removes any agency Leslie might have had
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is excellent: Leslie denies supporting Brandi's work → Brandi announces the porn parody → Leslie says please don't → it's already done. Each beat removes more of Leslie's control. 'Oh!' as Leslie's final horrified response is perfectly economical. The idea of a porn parody of a municipal bailout is exactly the kind of absurdist-but-grounded Parks joke that characterizes the show at its best.

jokes.text: The porn industry in town was really faltering. But now we're back. You're our hero!
jokes.setup: Brandi credits Leslie as a champion of Pawnee's adult film industry
jokes.punchline: Leslie is hailed as a hero for accidentally saving pornography
jokes.explanation: A solid extension of the Brandi/Leslie dynamic. The reveal that Pawnee has an industry-level porn economy and Leslie is its unlikely savior is a funny premise. 'You're our hero' while Leslie is mortified is good cringe structure.

jokes.text: No. To sing. / [Ann wants Chris talk but April leads them into 'Time After Time'] / Tell me about Chris. / [singing continues]
jokes.setup: Ann asks if April is ready to talk about the Chris situation
jokes.punchline: April deflects by starting to sing 'Time After Time' — using music as a hostage-situation escape from the emotional conversation
jokes.explanation: April using singing as deflection from an emotional conversation is a good character move — she'd rather have a genuine musical moment than talk about feelings. The forced friendship arc pays off here in a warm way that's also funny.

jokes.text: Tell me about Chris, or I'm leaving, and I don't care about the letter.
jokes.setup: April is singing instead of having the conversation Ann needs
jokes.punchline: Ann weaponizes the letter of recommendation to force the conversation — her leverage revealed
jokes.explanation: A decent callback to the letter leverage, but it's more story than joke. Works adequately as a comedic beat within the scene's dynamic.

jokes.text: This never happened.
jokes.setup: April and Ann have just had a genuine, warm musical moment together singing 'Time After Time'
jokes.punchline: April's immediate denial of any emotional connection — three words that try to erase the moment that just happened
jokes.explanation: One of the best three-word jokes in the episode. After a genuinely warm moment, April's reflexive denial is perfectly April — it would destroy her brand to have been caught being sincere. The economy is 10/10: three words do the work of a paragraph. The joke also works because the audience has watched her soften slightly, making her denial funnier and slightly bittersweet. The highest integration of character and economy in the episode.

jokes.text: I made everything worse. / If Tom were a bag of flour, that flour would never grow up to be a happy, well-adjusted loaf of bread. Much less a bran muffin, which is the highest honor that flour can achieve.
jokes.setup: Ben reflects on his parenting-Tom experiment in a talking head
jokes.punchline: He extends the flour metaphor to its logical extreme — a 'well-adjusted loaf of bread' and 'bran muffin as the highest honor' — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A standout callback joke. Ben has taken Ann's flour-sack metaphor and committed to it so deeply he's constructed an entire developmental hierarchy for baked goods. 'Bran muffin, which is the highest honor that flour can achieve' is an inspired absurdist escalation delivered with his characteristic earnestness. The specificity of bran muffin (not a croissant or a cake — a bran muffin) is a perfect comic choice. High originality.

jokes.text: You know, Chris, every parent makes mistakes. I mean, lord knows I've made plenty. But it's the small victories that keep you going... And another thing is if-- If, like-- If I-- You know, and then your kid's-- because you're like--vrrrr-- I don't know. / And everyone's like, 'Oh.' / Oh, I'm sorry, guys. I--no one ever lets me talk this long. I just got lost.
jokes.setup: Jerry is giving heartfelt parenting advice to Chris
jokes.punchline: He gets so flustered by being allowed to speak at length that he disintegrates into verbal noise ('vrrrr') and apologizes for losing the thread — he's so unused to having the floor
jokes.explanation: A great Jerry joke that's actually touching and funny simultaneously. The premise — Jerry is so accustomed to being interrupted that extended speaking time makes him lose his mind — is a perfect comedic use of his character's established dynamic. 'No one ever lets me talk this long' is the precise payoff, and the verbal disintegration ('vrrrr') is a great physical-comedy-in-dialogue moment.

jokes.text: It was a beautiful point. And very well said, right up until that moment that you started babbling incoherently. / And I'll have the number eight. / That's a party platter. It serves 12 people. / I know what I'm about, son.
jokes.setup: The group wraps up an emotional conversation at a restaurant
jokes.punchline: Ron orders a massive party platter for himself alone; when the waiter notes it serves 12, Ron's 'I know what I'm about, son' is imperious self-assurance about his appetite
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ron jokes in the episode. 'I know what I'm about, son' is an exceptional line — it's the exact right words, delivered with the exact right confidence, and it works completely independent of context. The waiter's straight-man moment makes it land harder. This is a highly quotable line that circulates far beyond this episode. Strong claim to best joke of the episode.

jokes.text: The free market is a jungle. It's beautiful and brutal and should be left alone. When a business fails, it dies, and a new, better one takes its place. Just let business be business and government be government. / [Ron gets the enormous party platter] / These will not be necessary. [gestures away the extra forks/plates]
jokes.setup: Ron gives his libertarian speech and the party platter arrives
jokes.punchline: He dismisses the extra place settings for 11 other people without breaking stride — he alone will consume this
jokes.explanation: The visual button on the Ron party-platter joke. 'These will not be necessary' dismissing 11 extra place settings is a perfect physical payoff. Combined with the preceding speech about individual freedom and self-reliance, the visual gag underlines his philosophy with perfect comic timing. This and Joke 69 form the strongest two-beat sequence in the episode.

jokes.text: I would suggest sticking around and watching him eat it 'cause it only takes four minutes, and it's pretty amazing. / These will not be necessary.
jokes.setup: Ron has ordered a party platter for 12 people for himself. Ben suggests watching Ron eat it as entertainment. Ron picks up the utensils the waitress has presumably left.
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the additional utensils — presumably extra forks, knives, plates for 12 people — as unnecessary. He doesn't need them. He will eat this alone, his way.
jokes.explanation: The button on the party platter joke. 'These will not be necessary' plus Ben's recommendation to watch Ron eat it in four minutes creates a vivid, funny image. The visual gag (Ron pushing aside the extra plates/utensils) is inferred from the dialogue but clear. The callback structure earns extra points because it deepens the joke about Ron's enormous and confident appetite.

jokes.text: I like capitalism. I love competition. I'm more competitive than you. / I don't think so. / I think so. / Settle down. / No, settle up. 'Cause the bill's been paid, and I've paid it, and I've won.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie's bickering escalates into a meta-competition about who is more competitive.
jokes.punchline: 'No, settle up' as a comeback to 'settle down' — Ron turns a cliché phrase into a victory claim, then immediately proves his point by asserting he won by paying the bill.
jokes.explanation: The 'settle up' wordplay is sharp and well-executed — it inverts the dismissal while making a point. Ron declaring victory because he paid is both petty and perfectly in character. The rapid-fire exchange ('I think so / I don't think so / settle down / settle up') has great rhythm.

jokes.text: Here is your letter of recommendation, so you're off the hook. No need to pretend to be my friend anymore. / Thank God.
jokes.setup: Ann releases April from the forced friendship agreement
jokes.punchline: April's immediate 'Thank God' — no hesitation, no gratitude, total relief
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical April beat. 'Thank God' is the only thing she says and it's the only thing she needs to say. Perfect character integration — any warmth that has developed is instantly denied.

jokes.text: I can't tell if you actually hate me or if this is just how you are, but I had fun hanging out with you. So I don't care what you say, you're my friend. And I hope you get into veterinary school because I like you, so there.
jokes.setup: Ann is officially ending the forced friendship week
jokes.punchline: Despite everything, she declares friendship anyway, ending with the defiant 'so there' — arguing a position into existence by sheer force of will
jokes.explanation: A warm joke that doubles as character revelation. 'So there' as a punctuation on a sincere declaration of friendship is funny because it sounds like a child's defiance. Ann's exasperated warmth vs. April's emotional walls has been the episode's B-arc and this closes it well.

jokes.text: We're gonna hug now. / No. / Yeah. / Ow! You're hurting me!
jokes.setup: Ann insists on a hug to seal the friendship
jokes.punchline: April complains she's being hurt by the hug, as if forced friendship has now become assault
jokes.explanation: A good physical button to the Ann-April arc. 'Ow! You're hurting me!' during a hug is perfectly April — she frames all warmth as violence. Short, sharp, character-specific.

jokes.text: Mm! Lot of hot 'D' in here tonight. Ooh, look at that chunky hunky. Go over there and talk to him and find out what his deal is. / No, I'm not gonna talk to some other guy. When we're together, you can't check out other guys. That's the deal.
jokes.setup: Tom and Mona-Lisa are at the client party together as a couple
jokes.punchline: She asks him to go hit on other men for her, and Tom has to establish that in a relationship, you don't scout on your partner's behalf
jokes.explanation: 'Chunky hunky' is a good Mona-Lisa coinage. Tom having to explain basic relationship parameters to someone who has never considered them is a solid character beat. 'Lot of hot D in here' as an opener is very in character — blunt to the point of absurdity.

jokes.text: Or else it's over between us, you understand? / Mm! Tommy laying down the law. A little feisty. I like that, okay? I'ma go get a soda. Do you want to have sex somewhere after I do that? / Sure.
jokes.setup: Tom gives Mona-Lisa an ultimatum about their relationship
jokes.punchline: She responds to his authority display the same way as before — with desire — and then immediately invites casual sex mid-party as if the conversation just ended
jokes.explanation: A solid callback to the authority-as-aphrodisiac joke. Tom's 'Sure' response to mid-party sex is the understated acceptance that seals the joke — he's now fully complicit. Good character consistency and callback payoff.

jokes.text: I think I'm gradually transforming her from truly terrible to only kinda terrible. It's the small victories, you know? / Indeed. / The small victories.
jokes.setup: Tom updates Ben on the Mona-Lisa situation
jokes.punchline: The 'small victories' callback ties to Ben's parenting-advice speech — Ben and Tom now share this phrase, though the victory being celebrated (slightly less terrible girlfriend) is deliberately underwhelming
jokes.explanation: A warm callback to Jerry's speech, now repurposed. 'Kinda terrible' as the goal state for a romantic partner is funny by understatement. Ben's 'Indeed. The small victories.' plays perfectly as him adopting the phrase now that it applies to something genuinely absurd.

jokes.text: I know she's kind of a monster, but whatever. I'm young. She's sexy. I'm just gonna see where this roller coaster goes.
jokes.setup: Tom explains his continued relationship with Mona-Lisa.
jokes.punchline: 'Kind of a monster' as the understatement of the episode — he's describing someone who commits arson threats, steals, and does ecstasy at work. 'Whatever. I'm young' as the philosophical framework.
jokes.explanation: 'Kind of a monster' as an acceptable relationship qualifier is a great understatement. Tom's 'I'm young' philosophy applied to dating actual monsters is funny and very Tom. Good economy.

jokes.text: Is there anything else you need help with? / Have you learned how to ride a bike yet? / Yeah. I'm 28 years old. / I'm proud of you, bud.
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom if there's anything else he needs
jokes.punchline: Ben asks if Tom can ride a bike — the most basic adult skill — then offers paternal pride when Tom confirms he can
jokes.explanation: A beautiful closing joke to the Ben-as-parent arc. 'Have you learned how to ride a bike yet?' at age 28 is a perfectly calibrated condescension disguised as care. Tom's offended 'Yeah. I'm 28 years old.' and Ben's 'I'm proud of you, bud' as sincere parental praise is the perfect button. Economical, warm, and completely earned. High quotability.

jokes.text: Ann Perkins. / Is that a happy 'Ann Perkins,' or is that a bad-news 'Ann Perkins'? / Oh, happy. Obviously. The bad-news one sounds like this. 'Ann Perkins.'
jokes.setup: Chris calls Ann's name; she asks how to read his tone
jokes.punchline: Chris demonstrates the two tonal registers of 'Ann Perkins' — happy vs. bad-news — which sound identical to everyone but him
jokes.explanation: A great Chris joke that also works on the meta-level: his 'Ann Perkins' interjection is itself a running gag in Parks, and this bit makes it explicit and self-aware. The joke works in text (both versions sound the same on the page) but is even funnier performed, as Pratt presumably uses identical delivery for both. Highly character-specific and quotable.

jokes.text: Well, I guess your uter-you and my uter-me are now our uter-us.
jokes.setup: Chris announces he'll donate sperm so Ann can have a baby
jokes.punchline: He constructs a uterus/pronoun pun: uter-you + uter-me = uter-us — a terrible but earnest wordplay
jokes.explanation: A characteristically Chris Traeger pun — optimistic, bodily, and genuinely attempting something clever. The uterus wordplay is anatomically specific and only he would deliver it this earnestly. 'Don't make me change my mind' is the perfect reaction. Improbably charming.

jokes.text: Don't make me change my mind.
jokes.setup: Chris delivers his uter-you/uter-me/uter-us pun
jokes.punchline: Ann's warning that the pun is putting the whole arrangement at risk
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the Chris pun. The idea that a wordplay could undo a life-altering reproductive decision is very funny. Ann's delivery of this as a sincere warning rather than a joke elevates it.

jokes.text: Although we are all sad and deeply grossed out that the Pawnee Videodome is turning into a porno palace, I am happy to announce that the Pawnee government will be hosting a weekly movie night here at the Community Center. Tonight's film is... The Sound of Music.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to salvage the community movie night idea from the porn shop disaster
jokes.punchline: 'Porno palace' — her prim language for the adult video store — followed by the contrast of The Sound of Music as the corrective
jokes.explanation: 'Porno palace' is a good Leslie-ism. The pivot to The Sound of Music as her corrective choice is perfectly Leslie — she overcorrects from porn to the most wholesome film imaginable. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The first community movie screening turns out to be the porn film Brandi Maxxxx made about Leslie — 'The Sound of Music' is announced but the porn plays. Leslie: 'I'm glad you're here, Dong Swanson. The local video store's about to go under. We have to save it.' Ron: 'I'm a strict libertarian, and I don't believe in bailouts.' Leslie: 'This is not how it happened.'
jokes.setup: Leslie hosts the first community screening, announces The Sound of Music.
jokes.punchline: The porn version featuring 'Dong Swanson' and a Leslie character begins playing. Leslie's breaking the scene by protesting 'This is not how it happened' is perfect — she's watching a porn of herself while the character also named Leslie objects to the fictional version.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best structured joke. 'Dong Swanson' as the Ron character's name is an inspired gag. The meta layers are stacked perfectly: (1) Leslie watches a porn of herself, (2) the porn has accurately captured the plot of the episode, (3) the fake Leslie in the porn objects to the bailout in the same scene, (4) real Leslie objects to the accuracy. 'This is not how it happened' from Leslie watching herself in a porn she was warned about but couldn't prevent is a perfect comedic endpoint. The structure earns a high score — this is a classic Parks cold close joke.

jokes.text: And... action. / I'm glad you're here, Dong Swanson. The local video store's about to go under. We have to save it. / Oh, this is the wrong movie. We ne-- shut this down, please. / Sorry, Leslie. / I'm a strict libertarian, and I don't believe in bailouts. / This is not how it happened.
jokes.setup: The movie night screens what turns out to be the porn parody of the Videodome bailout story
jokes.punchline: 'Dong Swanson' — the porn parody of Ron Swanson, whose character in the film gives the same libertarian anti-bailout speech — revealing the parody is faithful to the real events
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic climax and its best structural joke. 'Dong Swanson' is an exceptional porn-parody name (faithful phonetically and conceptually to 'Ron Swanson'). The joke then doubles down: 'Dong Swanson' delivers the SAME libertarian anti-bailout speech Ron gave earlier, which is both a perfect callback and an absurdist reveal that the porn parody is ideologically accurate. 'This is not how it happened' as Leslie's final protest is the perfect closing note — except it IS how it happened. A brilliantly constructed episode-closing joke.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is determined to help a local video store stay in business, while Chris offers Tom advice on how to deal with a difficult employee. Elsewhere, Ann resorts to blackmail to get April to be her friend.
insight: Budget crisis forces Leslie into absurd fundraising schemes; character comedy carries 78-point episode.
